1The keeper's first week

Standard work for a tree you are about to own.

Not a framework. Not advice. Not a demand.

This is one project's working arrangement, shown to you because you asked twice. Nothing in these slides asks you to believe anything — every claim has a date and a file in the tree behind me, and you can check any of them before deciding. What you leave with is a week's work, small enough to see all of.

2The premise

Things told to a session are lost — unless they are written down.

You remember little between months.

So: everything lives in the tree — and anything in the tree that is wrong will be believed.

This is the whole design. Whatever you tell a session is gone when the conversation ends; only what reaches the tree survives to the next one. I rediscovered within weeks that I have the same problem on a month's delay, and so does any stranger reading cold. One fix serves all three readers. Demonstrate, don't assert: open the tree, show a rule, show the test that holds it, break it, show the commit refused.

3The safety rule

Never open an unknown tree, or an unknown LLM session, on an unsafe machine.

The premise cuts both ways. A tree conditions whatever reads it — that is the point — so a tree written by someone else conditions your session just as well, including maliciously, and a session with tools is an actor, not a viewer: opening one inside an unknown tree executes that tree's intent on your machine. The rule you already have for running unknown code applies unchanged to the two new things. A strange tree is read as text, on a safe machine or in a sandbox, before any session is opened in it; and an unknown session gets a fence — mine denies its sessions' own sudo on purpose, and I can show the fence saying so. This practice is being reinvented elsewhere without this rule, and that is the unsafe version of it.

4Day zero — the first tasks

Before any ritual, three documents:

  • vision — what this is for
  • manifesto — how the work is done
  • author — what you spend attention on, and what each party owes

Then: let a session reflect on them, and discuss it with you.

These are my tree's names — vision.md, manifesto.md, spec/author.md — and yours may differ; the three questions they answer may not. Select or write first versions: short, dated, and a line earns its place by having decided something. Then the first act of the collaboration is not a task — it is handing the three to a session and talking them through. What the session reflects back shows you the gap between what the documents say and what you meant, while the gap is still cheap. And it is the honest start of the contract: the session learns what it is inside of, you learn what you actually wrote.

5The doubt

"I am really uncertain that I am up for this task."

— the author of the tree this comes from, 2026-08.

The doubt is the qualification.

That sentence is mine and it is in the public tree with a date. This method exists because its author distrusts his memory, his unmeasured claims and his own enthusiasm; the distrust, wired into files and a suite, is why it works. If you feel that doubt, you are holding the qualification, not the disqualification — the next slide is who actually fails.

6Known failures

the cargo-culter — copies the sentences, not the suite the metric abuser — feeds the number instead of the work * the mirror-shrine keeper — hears the tree echo him back, and calls it confirmation

What they share is confidence.

Every failure mode this method predicts for itself begins with somebody who was sure. Each of the three has a guard in my tree, built after a near-miss, with a date: copy-the-mechanisms-not-the-prose was measured, not preached — the prose-only copy failed its trial; a number nobody asked for is a number nobody checks, so no lamp is built ahead of its defect; and a session's praise of the method is the method grading itself, so the real checks are routed to strangers. Show one guard for real.

7Fix the task, not the person

When the job feels too big —

make the task smaller. Never the person bigger.

Held in the head, where doubt inflates it, keeping a tree is a fog. Written on a page it is five acts, thirty to sixty minutes. Toyota never asked for heroic operators; it wrote standard work so the job could be done on a tired Tuesday. This deck is the task, fixed — and when the doubt turns up mid-week, the answer is not introspection, it is go and look: your done-pile and journal will record the allegedly too-hard parts already being done, with dates. In this house it is written down which of those wins.

8The job, visibly small

actwhenabout
1. Read the lampsevery fire1 min
2. Open the decisions batchevery fire10–20 min
3. Measure one ruleevery fire10 min
4. One pass over the pileevery fire10 min
5. Rotate the journalwhen a lamp says — monthly30 min

Start with only one. Perfect it before adding the next.

Five acts, thirty to sixty minutes, weekly as a shape, not a law. But you do not start with five — you start with one, and my advice is act 1 the moment you own a lamp, because it is one minute and it teaches the posture: read the instrument, not your memory. Perfect one act — it happened, it was on the page, it produced its finding — before the next exists. The cadence is yours to move; what is not yours to move is doing them in the head instead of on the page.

9Three habits under everything

A claim with no file, test or number is unfinished.

A defect is a caller — the deliverable is the mechanism.

Go and look — before explaining, describe what it did.

These are the ground the five acts stand on, and they are most of the method. "It is fast" is not a statement; a millisecond count with the command that produced it is. When something breaks, a fix plus an apology is half the work — the other half is the check that makes that class of mistake fail loudly next time, usually a test under a second. And most confident explanations in my tree turned out wrong; there is a register of them, dated. Show the register.

10Act 1 — read the lamps. You have none yet.

One command, green or lit. A lit lamp is not a failure — it wants an act, not a panic, and it will still be lit next week.

Day one rule: build the instrument the moment the need arises.

In my tree this act is one command, twelve checks, fourteen seconds, and a page with two rows. You start with zero lamps and you do not build twelve — you build one: the cheapest check that would have caught your last mistake. That is how every lamp here was born; each one cites the defect that paid for it, and I can show you the ledger. A number nobody asked for is a number nobody checks — so never build a lamp ahead of its defect.

11Act 2 — decisions arrive shaped, or not at all

A question that reaches the keeper carries:

  • the question in one line
  • two or three named options, with costs
  • a default with a trigger — "if undecided by Friday, X"
  • reversibility stated
  • the recommendation marked suspected

Approving a default is ~10× cheaper than composing an answer.

A blank-page question is why decisions pile up. Most questions die before reaching you: half are already answered by the tree, and reversible-plus-measurable ones are experiments, not decisions — try, measure, keep or revert. What survives arrives shaped, and batched: five in one sitting cost less than five across a week. A blank question reaching you is a defect in whoever sent it — hold the sender to the shape, not yourself to the blank page.

12Act 3 — measure one rule against the week that happened

One rule. Not an audit.

Closed book first: write what it says from memory, then open it.

Three outcomes: it held · broken, nothing noticed · nobody could have followed it

Two of the three are findings.

Broken-and-nothing-noticed means the rule is prose, and the deliverable is a mechanism, not a resolution to be more careful. Nobody-could-have-followed-it means the rule is fat or wrong, and either way your rule budget gets a line back. The closed-book step is a reading on both your recall and the rule — one you cannot approximate from memory is one nobody could have followed, arriving early. Picking one rule is what makes this finishable; an audit is what makes it skipped.

13Act 4 — one pass over the shelf

One question per shelved card, and it is the only question:

Is this waiting on an event, or on me?

Event → sediment. Costs nothing. Leave it.

You → debt. It is not shelved, it is blocked on a decision. Move it into act 2.

A deep shelf is a rich board, not a fat one — but only half the time, and this pass is which half. The trap is tidying a debt card by re-shelving it with a better sentence. Show two real cards from my shelf, one of each kind, and let them sort a third.

14Act 5 — rotate the journal

Skim the closing month once. At heading level.

Promote only what a stranger needs to follow a rule — what they'd only need to believe it stays journal.

Most months promote nothing, and that is the expected result.

One index line. Close the file. Never rewrite the past.

Git already remembers; a retroactively edited journal is a second source of truth about the past, and my rules file names the refusal: archive, don't airbrush. My tree keeps its wrong entries corrected in place, with the correction dated — it teaches partly by visibly having been wrong, and so will yours.

15Kaizen — both parties learn from their mistakes

Four questions, at the end of a sitting:

what did we learn · what did we get wrong · what mechanism does that earn · what is tomorrow's first thing

The session asks you first — and waits.

A kaizen with one participant is a session grading itself.

The session's mistakes are cheap to catch — a measurement finds them. Yours are not: no suite can notice a choice made too fast, so this dialogue is the only instrument pointed at your half. Two rules keep it honest, both paid for in my tree with a date: the session asks and waits, because answers delivered first become the frame; and the entry is written only when both halves are in it. The third question is the one that turns talk into a tree — a lesson that earns no mechanism is a resolution, and resolutions do not survive a month.

16What this must never become

A demand.

No streak. No red gate for a missed evening. Skipping three weeks and doing one act on the fourth is the ritual working.

The tree that carries your values has to survive your absences, including the ordinary ones, or it is not safe to own. Build no reminder that fires unprompted; lamps speak when looked at, where you already stand. And a warning from my own tree, measured, not theoretical: the tree cannot supply conviction. What your project is for, which door, when to stop — that five per cent is structurally yours, and a tree that tells you otherwise is a mirror. Keep anchors that are not the tree.

17Everything you just saw is prose

Prose conditions by hope. A mechanism conditions by fact.

First question of any rule: what fails when it is broken?

Your deliverable this week is not notes on this talk. It is day zero, and your first gate.

These slides are the weakest form the method takes, and we measured that: a derived document of the method, handed alone to a reader with no tree, conditioned nobody — 2026-08-21, it is in the trial directory, kept as evidence. What transfers is the mechanism, never the sentences. So the homework: the three documents of day zero and the session dialogue over them; a board where every card states a problem and its because; one gate that refuses your last mistake; a journal file the rotation will one day close. And one act of the five, done once, on the page — perfected before the next. Next week we read your lamp — the one.
